summary: Source-anchored research for Sparse versus partial index equivalence. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: For a compound sparse index containing only ascending/descending keys, a document is indexed when at least one indexed field exists. Consequently, replacing sparse {a:1,b:1} with a partial filter requiring only b, or requiring both a and b, changes membership. Matching the documented inclusion rule requires an OR of the two existence tests; this is a logical derivation, not a guarantee of identical plans. (high confidence)

A partial index is eligible only when the query establishes its filter or a stricter subset; merely having a useful key pattern is insufficient. Percona demonstrates a false-only partial index being used for flag:false while flag:true takes a collection scan. (medium confidence)

SERVER-28889 records the redundant-filter FETCH improvement as fixed in 7.0.0-rc5 and 7.1.0-rc0. Its linked existence-predicate issue SERVER-26896 is separate, so that fix alone does not prove all existence-filter coverage cases are solved. This is the issue record updated 2026-09-21, not a claim about every later release. (low confidence)

For normal planner selection, a query must imply the partial filter, either by including it or a more restrictive condition. A query on an indexed field alone cannot generally use an index filtered on another field if matching documents outside the filter would be lost. (high confidence)
A sparse index normally cannot supply queries that need omitted documents. Forcing it with hint can return incomplete results, including an incorrect whole-collection count. (high confidence)

Partial filters can reference non-key fields and restrict values, so partial indexes support subsets that sparse:true cannot express. Mydbops illustrates an index on name filtered by existence of email. (medium confidence)

Historical evidence disproves blanket execution-plan interchangeability: SERVER-29247 reports extra FETCH work for partial-index counts in MongoDB 3.4.4; an independent Stack Overflow reproduction reports document fetches with partial filters in 4.2.1, 4.2.7 and 4.4.0-rc9. These reports establish historical behavior, not a current-version limitation. (medium confidence)

A MongoDB 2.6.5 user reported E11000 for a unique sparse {userId:1,name:1} index when repeated userId values paired with null name values. This is a historical first-hand failure example of mistaking compound sparsity for optional non-null uniqueness, rather than evidence of a current server defect. (low confidence)
An index definition cannot combine sparse and partialFilterExpression; a migration must create the desired alternative definition rather than turn on both options. (high confidence)

For a single ascending or descending field x, {x:1} with sparse:true has the same document-inclusion behavior as the same key with partialFilterExpression:{x:{$exists:true}}; MongoDB documents the partial form as supporting the same queries as the sparse form. (high confidence)

Existence is different from non-nullness: sparse indexes retain explicit null values and skip missing fields. The equivalent $exists:true partial filter also retains null; neither form means index only non-null values. (high confidence)

Partial indexes can filter on non-key fields and value conditions; for example, an index on city and surname can include only documents with age below 30. This is more expressive than the sparse presence rule. (high confidence)

A sparse unique index permits multiple documents omitting the indexed field but still indexes explicit null. With a partial unique index, uniqueness applies only to documents satisfying its filter; changing that filter changes the population subject to uniqueness. (high confidence)

Historical partial-index coverage limitations should be version-scoped: SERVER-28889 recorded an unnecessary FETCH for a predicate already guaranteed by a partial filter and lists fixes in 7.0.0-rc5 and 7.1.0-rc0. SERVER-26896 separately tracks covering $exists predicates. Equal index membership alone is insufficient evidence of an identical covered plan; inspect explain on the target server. (medium confidence)
The any-key rule does not extend unchanged to compound indexes containing geospatial or text keys; their documented sparse membership depends on the special-type fields. (low confidence)
